source.title: FuXi-$α$: Scaling Recommendation Model with Feature Interaction Enhanced Transformer
source.authors: Yu-Fei Ye; Wei Guo; Jin-Yao Chin; Hao Wang; Hong Zhu; Xi Lin; Yu-Yang Ye; Yong Liu; Rui-Ming Tang; De-Fu Lian; En-Hong Chen

record.tranche_reason: Applies scaling experiments to sequential recommendation models, a setting beyond text pretraining, and reports how recommendation metrics vary with model depth and width.
record.gate_note: The paper reports recommendation-ranking metrics across model sizes, not held-out cross-entropy or fitted power laws. The cited language-model scaling results are background only. The online A/B test and baseline comparisons do not test a scaling law; negative-sample-count results are not model-size scaling results.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a recommendation architecture motivated by scaling laws. Its scaling results are recommendation ranking metrics (NDCG@10, HR@10) against layer count and hidden dimension, mostly figure-only. It fits no power law, measures no held-out pretraining loss, makes no extrapolation and does no compute allocation. 'Adheres to the scaling law' here means only that performance rises with size. That can show monotone improvement but not the power-law form V5 names, so no version is tested. The sweeps mainly showcase the authors' own model.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude FuXi-α outperforms prior sequential recommenders and that its performance keeps improving with model size, which they call adhering to the scaling law. They also report depth gains that are dataset-dependent (a decline at 16 layers on MovieLens-1M, attributed to small data) and width saturation on MovieLens-1M.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales a sequential recommendation model and measures ranking metrics; it does not fit language-model held-out-loss power laws or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The depth trend differs by dataset: MovieLens-1M declines at 16 layers after improving to 8, whereas KuaiRand improves through 16 layers. Width performance saturates on MovieLens-1M but improves on KuaiRand.

fits_no_version.finding: FuXi-α ranking metrics rise with depth on Industrial (to 32 layers) and KuaiRand (to 16 layers). On MovieLens-1M they decline at 16 layers and saturate in hidden dimension at 32.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In sequential recommenders, ranking performance gains from model size are dataset-dependent and can saturate or reverse on small datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Going from 2 to 8 layers, SASRec degrades sharply on all three public datasets, while LLaMa, HSTU and FuXi-α improve on most (Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether a recommender benefits from added depth depends on architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing negative samples from 32 to 256 improves performance more than adding layers (Fig. 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In recommendation, training-objective settings such as negative-sample count can matter more than model size.

record.problems: The scaling curves are presented as figures without numeric values in the text; the reported scaling experiments use recommendation ranking metrics rather than held-out loss, and do not fit power laws.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 model comparisons, Table 3 industrial baseline comparisons, the ablation study, and the online A/B test were not extracted as scaling rows because they do not report the size-sweep outcomes targeted here. Negative-sample-count results are a training-setting sweep, not model-size scaling.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fit in parameters, data or compute.
No small-run fit used to predict larger runs.
Depth and width are swept separately, not at fixed parameter count; measures are ranking metrics, not loss.
Recommendation is a new setting, but no power-law form is fitted. Only a positive or saturating trend in ranking metrics is described (Figs 5-7).
No relation between scale or pretraining loss and downstream language tasks.
No exponents or compute-optimal splits are fitted or compared.

missing.what: Base (2-layer) vs Large (8-layer) comparisons for SASRec, LLaMa, HSTU and FuXi-α across three datasets; SASRec collapses (e.g. ML-20M NG@10 0.1375 to 0.0186).

record.verdict_notes: Changed the reader's relation from tests/T3 to uses_without_test/T4. The paper invokes scaling laws as motivation but reports no loss, no power-law fit and no numeric scaling values; Figures 5-7 are figure-only. Row links to 'none' are correct. There is a minor internal inconsistency: the abstract gives a 4.76% song-play gain, the A/B section 4.67%; this is not scaling-relevant.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship in parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run power-law fit is used to predict larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation or loss-minimising parameter/token split is tested.
Depth and width are varied, but the paper does not test their effects on held-out loss at fixed parameter count.
Recommendation is a different setting, but the paper does not fit or test the same power-law form; it reports ranking metrics against model size instead.
The paper reports recommendation-task metrics, not downstream-task performance predicted from pretraining loss or scale.

No scaling exponents or compute-optimal split are fitted or compared. Some recommendation metrics vary non-monotonically or saturate with depth or width, but these are not tests of fitted language-model power laws.
